title: The sheet of flowers, 1539
hook: tradition says that when Nanak died, Hindus and Muslims both claimed his body, and under the sheet they found only flowers

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tests of Lehna, and wet grass on fine clothes. Just do it well.

A funeral is about who a person was. It can also turn into a quarrel over who gets to say goodbye, and how. Kartarpur, 1539, by tradition's date. Guru Nanak is old now, and he's dying. Word spreads through the villages, and people come: Hindus who had followed him, and Muslims who had followed him. As they gather, a hard question rises. Hindus cremate their dead. Muslims bury theirs. So when the Guru is gone, which will it be? Who does he belong to?
screen: `WHO GETS TO SAY GOODBYE?` → `KARTARPUR, 1539.` → `HINDUS CREMATE. MUSLIMS BURY.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak heard the argument and settled it before it could start. Bring flowers, he said. Hindus, lay yours on my right side. Muslims, lay yours on my left. Whichever flowers are still fresh in the morning, that side may do as it wishes. Then he drew a sheet over himself, and died. In the morning his followers lifted the sheet. The body was gone. There were only the flowers, on both sides, and both were fresh. So, the story says, they cut the sheet in two. The Hindus cremated their half. The Muslims buried theirs. At Kartarpur today, there is a memorial and a grave, side by side. Sikhs hear this story in different ways. For some it's a miracle, a last sign. For others it's a picture of what the whole life meant. Either way, look at its shape. Remember his first words after the river: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. He didn't say that to erase anyone. Both groups kept their own ways; both grieved as their tradition taught. What he refused was to be owned by one side against the other. Even at the very end, he gave both sides something. Flowers for everyone. That's where Guru Nanak's story closes, twenty-two days of it: a boy at Talwandi, the river, the rebab, the road, Kartarpur. But he didn't leave the community without a leader. Before he died, he had already chosen who would carry the light, and given him a new name.
screen: `FLOWERS ON THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.` · `UNDER THE SHEET, ONLY FLOWERS.` · `THE SHEET CUT IN TWO.` · `NOT OWNED BY ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `FLOWERS FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Hold a flower, or a leaf or a picture if there's none handy, and think of where you'd lay it: a desk at work, a grave you haven't visited, the doorstep of a neighbor you don't know well, a shared kitchen. Let it be for someone whose goodness belongs to more than one group of people.
Phull. Flowers, the word behind the sheet Guru Nanak asked Hindus and Muslims to lay flowers on at his death, both halves found fresh by morning.
Your line: flowers for everyone. Tomorrow, the trader with the wet grass becomes Angad. That's day forty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's passing, traditionally dated 1539 at Kartarpur, where Gurdwara Darbar Sahib keeps both a samadh and a grave; the story of the flowers is told as a sign that he belonged to all people.

notes: Date of Guru Nanak's death: traditionally 1539 (22 September in common calendars; some sources give 7 September or other dates). Confirm.
The flowers story is janamsakhi tradition; details (right/left sides, cutting the sheet) follow common telling. Confirm.
Samadh and grave at Kartarpur (Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Narowal district): confirm current description.
'Twenty-two days' refers to Nanak's story running days 22–43 on this path.
